task: Write a toast for my sister's wedding. She is a nurse and her husband is a firefighter.
rewrite:
ambition:     A top speechwriter wouldn't just riff on "nurse + firefighter" jokes. They'd build the toast around one true, specific story about the sister (a moment that shows who she is) and let the couple's shared calling (running toward the worst day of other people's lives) land as the emotional turn, then end on a short, raisable-glass line.
agency:       The rawest material is the speaker's own memories: a real story about the sister growing up, how she and her husband met, something the husband did that proved who he is, and the speaker's own words for how they feel about her. None of that is in reach right now, so I'll write with a clearly marked placeholder for one anecdote and assume a warm, lightly funny tone for a mixed-age crowd, about 2 minutes (roughly 300 words).
acceleration: Use the standard toast structure that works: open with who you are and a quick hook, one story, a turn that ties it to the couple, a wish for them, then "please raise your glass." Use the rule of three for the wishes, and read it aloud once with a timer to trim to under 2 minutes.
accuracy:     Nothing outside the model can verify a toast is right except the speaker and the room. The closest proxies: the sister (or a friend who knows her) reads it for facts and tone, and the speaker reads it aloud once to check timing and that every line sounds like something they would actually say.

answers.plain:
Here's a toast you can adapt. I've left brackets where personal details will make it land better.

---

**Wedding Toast**

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm [Name], [Bride]'s [older/younger] sibling.

I've thought a lot about what to say tonight, and I kept coming back to this: my sister spends her days taking care of people at their most vulnerable, and [Groom] spends his running toward the places everyone else is running away from. Between the two of them, they've got the whole "saving the day" thing covered.

[Bride], you've been the caretaker of our family for as long as I can remember. [Add a short, specific memory: a time she looked after you, a sick day, a late-night phone call.] It doesn't surprise me at all that you chose a career where compassion is the job. You show up, you stay calm, and you make everyone around you feel like things will be okay.

[Groom], when you came into our lives, it was clear very quickly that you were someone who shows up too. [Add a short detail: how he won the family over, a moment you realized he was the one for her.] Thank you for loving my sister the way she deserves.

Now, I have to say, these two have the most dramatic "meet-cute" potential of any couple I know. One of them can handle an emergency room, and the other can handle an actual fire. I'm fairly sure that means our family never has to worry about a thing, as long as nobody asks either of them to cook dinner.

But seriously, what I admire most about the two of you is that you've both chosen lives of service. You know how short and precious life can be, and you don't take a single day for granted. That's the kind of awareness that makes for a strong marriage.

So here's my wish for you both: may your shifts line up more often than not, may your home always be the calm after the storm, and may you always find your way back to each other, no matter how long the day was.

Everyone, please raise your glasses.

To [Bride] and [Groom]: may your love be steady, your hearts stay strong, and your life together be everything you've hoped for.

Cheers!

---

If you tell me a few things, I can personalize it further: your relationship with her (older or younger, close or teasing), the tone you want (sentimental, funny, or a mix), a favorite story about the two of them, and roughly how long you'd like to speak. This version runs about 90 seconds to two minutes.

# Wedding Toast

*About 2 minutes spoken. Bracketed items are slots for your details.*

---

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm [Name], [Bride]'s [older/younger] sibling. I've known her my whole life, which means I'm qualified to tell you three things about her: she's the person you want in the room when something goes wrong, she will absolutely tell you what to do about it, and she's usually right.

[Bride] became a nurse because she was always going to. Even as a kid, [one-line true story: she bandaged the dog, ran the "clinic" in the living room, took charge when someone got hurt]. Now she does it for a living, often at 3 a.m., for strangers on the worst days of their lives. She's the calm voice and steady hands, and the person who remembers to ask whether the family has eaten.

And then there's [Groom].

[Groom] became a firefighter, which means that when most people hear an alarm and think *get out*, he thinks *I'll go in.*

When I realized who they each were, it made a strange kind of sense. Most of us spend our lives hoping we never meet the people in their line of work. They spend theirs hoping to meet the rest of us on our worst day, and to make it a little better.

They're also a perfect match for practical reasons. Neither one has ever said "but it's 4 a.m." as an excuse. Both can sleep anywhere, instantly, in any position. And [Groom] is the first partner she's had who doesn't blink when she says "I've been up for 26 hours, I'm fine." He just hands her a sandwich and says, "I know."

[Optional personal beat, 2-3 sentences: the moment you knew he was right for her. Something specific, such as how he acted the first time he met the family, or something he did when she was exhausted.]

Here's what I've noticed watching them together. Their whole careers are about showing up for people in crisis. At home, they show up for each other without anyone asking. [Bride], you've found someone who runs toward the hard thing, and who will also do the dishes after a double shift. [Groom], you've married someone who knows how to take care of everyone, and you're going to be the one who gets to take care of her.

So in a marriage between a nurse and a firefighter, I'm not worried. If anyone knows how to handle emergencies, it's these two. I just hope that most of the days ahead are boring ones: quiet mornings, lazy Sundays, no pagers, and a shared couch.

Everyone, please raise your glass.

To [Bride] and [Groom]: may your shifts line up, your days off be long, and your home always be the safest place either of you knows.

**To the happy couple!**

---

## Notes to make it yours

- **Fill in the two personal slots first.** One specific, true story beats any polished line. Keep each to 3 sentences or fewer.
- **Check the humor with the couple or a trusted friend.** The "26 hours" joke and the sleeping joke are safe, but swap them for real habits of theirs if you know any.
- **Pacing:** pause after "I'll go in" and after "the worst day." Those are the lines that land, so don't rush them.
- **Cutting for time:** drop the "practical reasons" paragraph for a ~90-second version.
- **Delivery:** print it large or use cards, and rehearse out loud twice. Hold the glass only for the final line.

If you give me their names, how you're related, and one or two real anecdotes, I can tailor it, adjust the tone (funnier, more sentimental, shorter), or write a version for a specific length.
answers.skill:
# Wedding Toast (about 300 words, roughly 2 minutes)

**Hook**
Good evening, everyone. I'm [YOUR NAME], [SISTER]'s [brother / sister / sibling]. I've known her my whole life, so I have a lot of stories. Tonight, you only get one. She approved it. Mostly.

**Story**
**[STORY SLOT: about 85 words, roughly 35 seconds. Drop in your real memory here. Cover:**
**1. When and where it happened (one sentence).**
**2. What she did, in plain action.**
**3. One small detail only you would know: something she said, did, or refused to make a fuss about.**
**4. How it ended.]**

That's my sister. She doesn't make a fuss. She just shows up.

**Turn**
And that's what her work is: showing up on people's worst days. [HUSBAND] does the same thing, in a different uniform. Most people back away from the worst day. These two walk toward it. So when they found each other, I wasn't surprised. I was relieved. People who spend all day taking care of everyone else deserve someone who takes care of them.

**Three wishes**
So, three wishes.
First: may you have lots of boring days. Quiet mornings, no emergencies, nothing to report.
Second: on the hard days, and there will be some, may you be each other's first call.
Third: may you keep laughing together as easily as you do today, even when you're tired. And you will be tired.

**Raise your glass**
Everyone, please raise your glass. To [SISTER] and [HUSBAND]: thank you for always showing up. Now go enjoy your good day. Cheers!

---

**Assumptions**
- **Names:** [SISTER] and [HUSBAND] are placeholders. I didn't guess at names, and I kept "husband" out of any pronoun use so nothing needs fixing.
- **Tone:** Warm, with light humor ("She approved it. Mostly." and "you will be tired"). No job-based jokes, as you asked.
- **Time together:** I didn't state a length. The toast works for any amount of time. If it's been years, you could add "I've watched this for [X] years" to the turn.
- **Length:** Without the story, the toast runs about 215 words. An 85-word story brings it to about 300, so keep your story near that size.
- **Facts to confirm:** The only claims are that she's a nurse, he's a firefighter, and she's okay with the story you choose. Your sister or a close friend should check the story and the "doesn't make a fuss" line.

**For timing:** Read it aloud with a timer once the story is in. If you run over, trim the story first, not the wishes.

**The one thing that would sharpen it most:** the story you'd tell about your sister. The best version is a small moment where she took care of someone without being asked or thanked, ideally outside of work. It could be a time she showed up for you, a friend, or a stranger. If you tell me the moment in a few rough sentences, I'll tighten it to fit the slot and tune the bridge line to match.
